tech_policy.headline: The government took a frontier model offline.
evidence: US Commerce directive suspended foreign access to Fable 5 / Mythos 5; Anthropic disabled both for all users
Amazon CEO Jassy triggered it; Anthropic called vulns 'previously known' and 'minor'
'Open source AI must win' trending as the local-weights reaction

tech_policy.implication: The order applies to all foreign nationals, including some of Anthropic's own staff, rather than only to foreign customers.
tech_policy.summary: On June 12, the US Commerce Department ordered Anthropic to suspend access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all foreign nationals on national-security grounds, and the company disabled both models for every customer to comply. Reporting traces the order to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy, who told officials that Amazon researchers had coaxed Fable 5 into producing material useful for cyberattacks; Anthropic called the flaws already known and minor. It appears to be the first time a frontier model has been pulled offline by government order rather than a company's own choice.

After a year of expected easing, the major central banks have turned together toward tightening, driven by the same sticky, energy-led inflation. At the same time the industry is in its worst memory shortage in about fifteen years, as high-bandwidth memory for AI pulls capacity away from everything else, and power-capacity prices sit at record caps. Capacity is now rationed by power and memory, not silicon.

structural_regimes.name: The AI margin question
structural_regimes.read: The economics of AI became the argument of the week. xAI shipped Grok 4.5 at roughly sixty percent below comparable frontier input prices, and a viral thesis held that cheap open-weights models will collapse the fat gross margins of closed AI services. The rebuttal, that inference is quietly profitable even at low prices, is unproven either way. What is clear is that price, not just capability, is now the battleground.

structural_regimes.name: Global rearmament
structural_regimes.read: The West put money behind its security worries. At the NATO summit in Ankara on July 7 and 8, allies reaffirmed a target of five percent of GDP on defense by 2035 and committed about seventy billion euros in military aid to Ukraine for 2026, with the US offering a production license for Patriot interceptors. NATO says European members and Canada have added more than a hundred and thirty billion dollars of defense investment since last year. Rearmament is now a durable driver of budgets and industrial policy, and it runs straight into the critical-minerals squeeze.

structural_regimes.name: Digital ownership and the right to repair
structural_regimes.read: Who controls what you buy became a live legal question. The FTC and five states settled with John Deere on July 8, binding it for ten years to give farmers and independent repair shops the same tools and software it gives its dealers, a rare win for buyers. It cuts against the drift the other way, where a purchase increasingly buys a revocable license, as Sony's move to end physical discs for new games in 2028 underlined. Ownership is being renegotiated, sometimes toward the buyer and sometimes away.

ai_compute.headline: The open-model race reopens, and China is setting the pace.
ai_compute.summary: Moonshot released Kimi K3 on July 16, a 2.8 trillion parameter model priced at $3 per million input tokens with open weights promised by July 27, and it topped Hacker News at 2,100 points. Thinking Machines shipped Inkling a day earlier, an Apache-licensed release that now leads the American open-weights field. Alibaba previewed Qwen 3.8 at the World AI Conference in Shanghai, where Xi Jinping championed open-source AI and 29 countries founded a new AI cooperation body. Bloomberg reported Z.AI annualizing near a billion dollars, a first for a Chinese lab.

deep_dive.headline: Neural implants restore touch while Washington decides who pays for clinical AI.
deep_dive.summary: Researchers at Northwell's Feinstein Institutes reported in Nature Medicine that a double neural bypass, five electrode arrays stimulating brain and spinal cord together, restored touch and movement to Keith Thomas, paralyzed since 2020 (STAT, July 16). The money side moved the same week: Medicare proposed a Software as a Medical Service payment category in its 2027 physician fee rule, and a Senate bid to end its AI prior-authorization pilot failed 46 to 50. The FDA also approved Merck's Lipfendra, the first oral PCSK9 cholesterol pill.
deep_dive.implication: The Senate resolution to end Medicare's six-state AI prior-authorization pilot failed 46 to 50 on July 16, so the test continues.

geopolitics.headline: An oil shock out of the Gulf, and the lights go out from Crimea to Chile.
geopolitics.summary: Satellite images published July 17 showed fresh damage inside Iran's Bushehr nuclear plant, and US marines boarded a tanker in the Gulf of Oman as the naval blockade tightened; Brent settled Friday at $86.72, up about 14 percent on the week. Iran said the June memorandum with Washington is suspended. Ukraine's strike campaign cut Crimea's power and fuel links to Russia. Beyond those theatres, the UN called for investigations into at least 31 deaths in Pakistani-administered Kashmir, and a winter storm left roughly half a million Chilean customers without power.

markets.headline: An oil spike ends the record run, but the flight to safety never came.
markets.summary: The S&P 500 fell about 1.6 percent from its record and the VIX, a gauge of expected swings, rose about 25 percent to near 19. The trigger was energy: US crude rose about 14 percent on Gulf escalation. It was not a full risk-off week, though. Gold fell about 2 percent, silver 6, and bitcoin held flat, so money left oil-exposed trades without running to shelter. Growth trackers cooled, with GDPNow near 1.7 percent, into the Federal Reserve's July 28-29 meeting. Directional only, not investment advice.

commodities.summary: Energy led as Gulf tensions flared: Brent settled at $86.72 and WTI at $81.43, both up about 14 percent on the week. Wheat rose 8 percent on European heat. The softs went the other way, cocoa down 6.5 percent and coffee 4.2, and silver fell 6.3 percent. The forward question is whether an energy-led inflation scare reaches the Federal Reserve on July 28-29.

undercurrent.headline: Developers negotiate terms with the machine, in both directions.
undercurrent.summary: Andrew Kelley, Zig's creator, disputed Anthropic's framing of its AI-assisted rewrite of Bun from Zig to Rust, and the post drew 1,550 points on Hacker News. An Ask HN thread asking for a flag on AI-generated articles drew about 1,100 more. The counterweight came from Linus Torvalds, who wrote on a kernel list that Linux is not an anti-AI project and that he would refuse attempts to ban AI tooling. The argument is no longer whether to use the machine but on whose terms.

wildcard.headline: The largest leveraged buyout in history clears its European gate.
wildcard.summary: Reuters reported July 17 that the Saudi PIF-led consortium, with Affinity Partners and Silver Lake, is set to win EU approval for its 55 billion dollar take-private of Electronic Arts, announced last September as the largest leveraged buyout on record. The notable part is the gate itself: the decisive review ran under the EU's foreign-subsidies rules, scrutinizing Saudi state backing rather than competition, with clearance expected by July 30. A US national-security review stays open into late September.
